newsitem.title: USA: Bridgeport, Conn asks state treasurer to apologize.
newsitem.headline: Bridgeport, Conn asks state treasurer to apologize.

text.p: Bridgeport, Connecticut's mayor, fearing negative comments made by the state treasurer, Christopher Burnham, would make it more costly for it to sell bonds, on Wednesday demanded an apology from Burnham.

Saying the state treasurer had "grossly distorted" its unfunded pension liability and financial outlook, Mayor Joseph Ganim said: "Your comments may have hurt our ability to further boost the city's bond rating, thereby costing Bridgeport's taxpayers another opportunity to save money as we continue to improve the city's roads, schools and other infrastructure."

Ganim, who came into office on a platform to rescue Bridgeport's finances after it went into bankruptcy in 1991, made his comments in a letter to Burnham that he released. He said Burnham made his remarks last week at a meeting by the Government Finance Officers Association in Cromwell.

Bridgeport, the state's biggest city with 140,000 residents, plans to sell up to $50 million of debt in 30 days to pay for various capital projects. Located on Long Island Sound, about 20 miles southwest of New Haven, the city will use some of the funds to spur development on the waterfront.

A spokesman for the state treasurer said that Burnham's remarks must be viewed in the context of a much broader concern about the 169 Connecticut towns that face approximately $1.6 billion of unfunded pension liabilities.

Two towns, Stratford and New Britain, have each gotten approval to sell approxmately $100 million of bonds to finance these liabilitiies, according to the spokesman. He noted the treasurer and a task force set up by the legislature were analyzing the problem and trying to devise solutions.

The state treasurer, in prepared remarks, said: "I have a deep concern about how Bridgeport and other municipalities have managed their pension funds in the past. We are conducting our own internal analysis of those municipal pension funds and expect that that exercize will be complete within a month or so."

Bridgeport's mayor, in his letter, pointed out the state of Connecticut has about $6 billion to $7 billion of unfunded pension liabilities. The treasurer's spokesman said Burnham, who takes a cautious approach towards bonding out such problems, was not planning to use that approach.

Bridegeport has the biggest issue with unfunded pension liabilities of all the Connecticut towns, Burnham's spokesman said, adding its unfunded pension liability totaled about $355 million. This figure exceeded a $250 million to $260 million estimate provided by Ganim, the mayor, and no explanation for the discrepancy was immediately available. Ganim added he does not plan to sell bonds to finance the city's liability.
Burnham's spokesman said the treasurer would not apologize for his comments "Because there is no need to."

Standard and Poor's last spring gave the city a BBB-minus rating, with a positive outlook, a judgment expected to last one to three years, according to Robin Prunty, a municipal analyst with the firm. "That doesn't mean the rating will be raised," she said, adding the agency tentatively plans to release its latest review next week.
